design_detail: Repeated cross-sectional analysis of five annual waves (2015 to 2019) of the US National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), 195,711 respondents aged 18 to 64, combined with counts of overdose deaths involving psychostimulants other than cocaine from the National Vital Statistics System Multiple Cause of Death files for the same years. Outcomes: past-year methamphetamine use, methamphetamine use disorder, injection, frequent use (100 or more days), and their correlates, estimated with survey-weighted multinomial and binary logistic regression.
can_establish: National estimates and year-on-year trends in self-reported past-year methamphetamine use, use disorder, injection and frequent use among non-institutionalized US adults aged 18 to 64, the mutually adjusted cross-sectional associations of those patterns with social and clinical characteristics, and the parallel trend in recorded psychostimulant-involved overdose deaths.
cannot_establish: Any causal or individual-level link between the survey trends and the death counts: the two data sources describe different populations (survey respondents versus decedents) and are never linked, so the paper cannot show that the people whose use patterns changed are the people who died. It also cannot capture people excluded from the survey frame (unsheltered homeless, incarcerated, military), cannot verify self-report, and cannot distinguish methamphetamine from other psychostimulants in the mortality data.

sample.recruitment: Probability sample of the US civilian non-institutionalized population aged 12 and over, interviewed in person at households and non-institutional group quarters, with audio computer-assisted self-interviewing for sensitive items. Analysis restricted to respondents aged 18 to 64. Mortality data are national death certificates, not a sample.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Survey respondents aged 18 to 64 in the 2015 to 2019 waves. Earlier years were excluded because NSDUH method changes created a trend break in 2015. Overdose deaths were those with an underlying-cause ICD-10 code of X40-X44, X60-X64, X85 or Y10-Y14 and a mention of T43.6 (psychostimulants with abuse potential other than cocaine), among decedents aged 18 to 64.
sample.demographics: Weighted: 50.9% women, 49.1% men; 18.0% Hispanic, 12.6% Black, 60.6% White. Age, education, income, insurance, marital status, metropolitan status, probation or parole, housing moves, medical diagnoses, depression, suicidality and other substance use were all measured and used as covariates.
sample.attrition: Annual mean weighted screening response rate 75.3% and interview response rate 67.3% for 2015 to 2019, implying an overall weighted response of roughly 51% (editors' calculation). Non-response is handled by the survey weights; no further information on differential non-response is given.
sample.selection_effects: The survey frame excludes people experiencing unsheltered homelessness and people who are incarcerated or otherwise institutionalized, groups with more drug use and higher overdose risk; the authors state this probably causes underestimation. Sensitive behaviour is self-reported with no biological verification, so recall and social-desirability bias apply. The mortality denominator is the whole population, while the survey estimates come from the non-institutionalized population, so the two series are not strictly comparable.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in the NSDUH audio computer-assisted interview: past-year methamphetamine use and number of days of use; past-year injection of methamphetamine (also heroin and cocaine); and a past-year methamphetamine use disorder derived from DSM-IV criteria as implemented by NSDUH. The paper labels this 'methamphetamine use disorder (MUD)' and describes its symptoms in DSM-5 terms, but the stated diagnostic source is DSM-IV, that is abuse or dependence as operationalized in the survey. No biological verification.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequent use was defined as 100 or more days of methamphetamine use in the past 12 months. Route was captured only as injection versus not; smoking, snorting and oral use are not distinguished. Quantity, dose and purity are not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Measured in detail and entered as covariates: past-year cocaine, cannabis (use disorder or daily to near-daily use), hallucinogen use, heroin use or prescription opioid misuse, prescription tranquilizer, sedative and stimulant misuse, heroin injection, past-month nicotine dependence (Nicotine Dependence Syndrome Scale), and alcohol use and use disorder (dropped from the final models for the use, disorder and injection outcomes because they were not associated with those outcomes; alcohol use disorder was retained in the frequent-use model). Mortality analyses separate deaths involving psychostimulants with and without opioids and with and without cocaine.

comparison.controls: Within the survey, respondents with no past-year methamphetamine use serve as the reference category for the three use outcomes; within the frequent-use analysis, people who used methamphetamine without a use disorder or injection are the reference. Each covariate has its own reference level (for example Black respondents for race and ethnicity, private insurance for coverage, no probation or parole).
comparison.matching: None; adjustment is by multivariable regression with all listed covariates entered simultaneously. The paper reports that multicollinearity and interaction effects were tested and not found.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense, but the cross-sectional design means that the direction of every association is unknown: depression, suicidal ideation, infection, housing instability and criminal-justice involvement may precede, follow or coincide with methamphetamine use. No temporal ordering is available.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The reference group for each outcome is everyone else in the survey, including people using other drugs; other substance use is adjusted for rather than excluded.

outcomes.instruments: NSDUH self-report items for substance use, injection and days of use; NSDUH DSM-IV substance use disorder algorithms; NSDUH DSM-IV past-year major depressive episode; Nicotine Dependence Syndrome Scale; self-reported physician diagnoses (hypertension, heart disease, diabetes, cancer, COPD, asthma, hepatitis B or C, HIV/AIDS, past-year sexually transmitted infection); self-reported probation or parole, residential moves and suicidality. Mortality: ICD-10 coded death certificates.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite published validation and reliability work for the NSDUH substance-use and disorder measures. They note that about 85% to 90% of death certificates mentioning psychostimulants other than cocaine mention methamphetamine, and that about 6% of overdose death certificates in 2019 named no specific drug, so the death counts are a proxy and an undercount.
outcomes.operationalization: Three mutually exclusive use categories (use without disorder or injection; use disorder without injection; injection regardless of disorder) plus frequent use (100 or more days). 'Overdose death' follows the ICD-10 coding above; deaths from methamphetamine-associated conditions such as stroke or myocardial infarction are not counted, which the authors say makes total methamphetamine-associated mortality markedly underestimated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated. Four outcome models, each with roughly 20 covariates and many levels (Tables 2 to 4 together report several hundred adjusted estimates), plus trend tests on 18 series in Table 1 with linear, quadratic, cubic and quartic forms tested; all at two-sided P<0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; computer-assisted self-report and administrative death records.

analysis.effect_sizes: Survey-weighted counts with 95% CIs, adjusted prevalences, and adjusted risk ratios with 95% CIs from multivariable multinomial logistic regression (SUDAAN 11.0.3, accounting for the complex design). Deaths involving psychostimulants other than cocaine rose from 5,526 in 2015 to 15,489 in 2019 (+180%). Survey counts (thousands, 95% CI): any past-year use 1,612 (1,394-1,829) in 2015, 1,381 (1,193-1,568) in 2016 and 1,971 (1,660-2,282) in 2019; use disorder 741 (578-905), 672 (539-805) and 1,091 (816-1,365); use disorder without injection 549 (417-682), 397 (299-496) and 815 (598-1,033); injection 321 (224-418), 388 (277-498) and 365 (257-473), with no significant linear trend (P=0.07, quadratic); frequent use 649 (551-747), 615 (512-717) and 1,021 (860-1,183). The headline percentage increases in the abstract are computed from the lowest year rather than from 2015 (see reporting issues): editors' calculations from Table 1 give 2015-to-2019 changes of +22% for any use, +47% for use disorder, +48% for use disorder without injection, +57% for frequent use, +6% for use without disorder or injection and +60% for methamphetamine with cocaine. Strongest adjusted associations (adjusted risk ratios vs the stated reference): heroin injection with methamphetamine injection 9.97 (6.43-15.47); American Indian or Alaska Native versus Black respondents for use disorder without injection 9.98 (4.16-23.95); probation or parole 4.26 (3.25-5.58) for use disorder without injection; HIV/AIDS 4.50 (2.60-7.80); Hispanic versus Black 5.13 (2.72-9.66); homosexual men versus heterosexual women for injection 3.66 (2.17-6.16); cannabis and cocaine use around 2.4 to 3.4; opioid misuse 2.18 to 3.40; nicotine dependence 1.87 to 2.08; three or more residential moves 3.02 (2.25-4.05) for injection. Among people who used methamphetamine, frequent use was more likely with a use disorder (adjusted prevalence 53.84%, adjusted risk ratio 1.65, 1.42-1.92) or injection (52.68%, 1.62, 1.35-1.94) than with use alone (32.59%).
analysis.covariates: Age group, sex and sexual orientation, race and ethnicity, education, household income, health insurance, number of residential moves, metropolitan status, probation or parole, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis B or C, past-year sexually transmitted infection, past-year major depressive episode, past-year suicidal ideation, past-month nicotine dependence, cannabis, cocaine, hallucinogen, opioid, tranquilizer or sedative and prescription stimulant misuse, and heroin injection. Alcohol measures were dropped from the three-category model for lack of association and retained in the frequent-use model.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or analysis plan is referenced. The data are secondary; analyses were run between 8 February and 8 March 2021.
analysis.selective_reporting: Bivariable results are in an unread supplement. The discussion cites an 'additional analysis' of overdose deaths by age group whose numbers are not reported anywhere in the paper. The trend tests report whichever of linear or quadratic forms applied, with cubic and quartic forms tested and not found.
analysis.power: Not discussed. Precision varies greatly: national counts for any use are relatively precise, whereas subgroup adjusted prevalences for small groups (Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, Asian, respondents with unknown sexual orientation) have intervals spanning several-fold ranges, for example an adjusted risk ratio of 9.98 (4.16-23.95).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Between 2015 and 2019, recorded US overdose deaths involving psychostimulants other than cocaine rose nearly threefold (5,526 to 15,489) among adults aged 18 to 64, while self-reported past-year methamphetamine use in the non-institutionalized population rose much less, and the composition of use shifted towards use disorder, frequent use and co-use with cocaine. Injection did not increase significantly. From 2017 onwards, most people reporting past-year use had a use disorder or injected (60% to 67%) rather than using without either (37% to 40%). In cross-section, use, use disorder and injection were each associated with lower education and income, lack of private insurance, housing instability, probation or parole, infections, depression, suicidal ideation and other drug use; adjusted prevalence of use disorder rose in every demographic group examined, with the largest proportional rise among Black respondents (0.06% to 0.64% between the 2015-2017 and 2018-2019 periods).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions state that the study found riskier patterns of use and rapidly diversifying populations at risk during a time of increasing overdose mortality, and the Key Points ask whether trends in use among vulnerable populations are 'associated with' increases in overdose mortality. Gaps: (1) the survey and the death counts are never linked, so the parallel trends are ecological; the discussion's statement that the results 'help explain' the rise in deaths goes beyond what two unlinked series can show; (2) the headline growth figures (43% for use, 105% for use disorder without injection, 66% for frequent use, 42% for use without disorder or injection) are calculated from the lowest year in the series, usually 2016 and once 2017, while being described as changes from 2015, which roughly doubles the apparent growth for several measures; (3) the abstract presents the subgroup increases as 'from 2015 to 2019' although the results section compares the pooled 2015-2017 period with 2018-2019; (4) 'methamphetamine use disorder' is measured by DSM-IV criteria but named and described with DSM-5 language; (5) the risk-factor list is cross-sectional and the direction of each association is unknown, which the limitations state but the abstract's phrase 'risk factors included' does not convey.

timeline.event: Palamar, Han and Keyes report changing characteristics of people who use methamphetamine in the US, 2015 to 2018 (cited as reference 7).

Jones and colleagues report rising methamphetamine use among heroin treatment admissions and resurgent methamphetamine use at treatment admission, 2008 to 2017 and 2008 to 2017 (cited as references 8 and 9).

Han and colleagues report methamphetamine overdose deaths by sex and race and ethnicity, with the fastest increases among Black men, 2011 to 2018 (cited as reference 2; overlapping authors and data sources).
This study: 2015 to 2019 NSDUH and National Vital Statistics System.

replication.where_it_stands: The survey trends come from a single national data source with a trend break in 2015 and are reported by an author group at the funding agency that also publishes the related mortality analyses, so the companion papers are not independent. The direction of the findings (deaths rising far faster than reported use, growth concentrated in use disorder and in groups not historically affected) is consistent with treatment-admission and death-certificate studies cited in the paper. Later NSDUH waves (2020 onward) would be needed to say whether the trends continued.

funding.funder: Sponsored by the National Institute on Drug Abuse of the National Institutes of Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The paper states the sponsors reviewed and approved the manuscript but had no role in design, conduct, data handling, analysis, manuscript preparation or the decision to submit.
funding.declared_conflicts: One author reported long-term stock holdings in General Electric, 3M and Pfizer outside the submitted work; no other disclosures.
funding.affiliations_note: Four of the five authors, including the NIDA director, are at the National Institute on Drug Abuse; the fifth is at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The sponsoring agencies are the authors' employers and reviewed and approved the manuscript, which is unusual enough to record: the paper's policy recommendations are those of the agencies that fund the field. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the estimates.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: A national probability frame for US civilian non-institutionalized adults, but it excludes people who are incarcerated, institutionalized or unsheltered, among whom methamphetamine use and overdose risk are higher; the authors state this causes underestimation.
Multistage probability sampling with in-person household and group-quarters interviewing and survey weights.

195,711 respondents give precise national estimates, but subgroup adjusted estimates (Asian, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, respondents with unknown sexual orientation, and the 0.06% baseline for Black respondents) rest on small numbers with intervals spanning several-fold ranges.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Tables 1 to 4 and the methods describe the population, years, measures and covariates; NSDUH methods are referenced.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Weighted screening response 75.3% and interview response 67.3% (about 51% overall, editors' calculation); weights adjust for non-response but no non-response bias analysis is reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Self-report with audio computer-assisted self-interviewing and validated NSDUH disorder algorithms, but no biological verification, and the disorder construct is DSM-IV while labelled and described as DSM-5. The mortality outcome is an ICD-10 proxy (T43.6) in which 85% to 90% of certificates mention methamphetamine.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same instrument and mode across all waves; the authors restrict the analysis to 2015 onward precisely because earlier waves are not comparable.

Complex-survey estimation in SUDAAN with weighted counts, adjusted prevalences and adjusted risk ratios, with collinearity and interactions checked; but percentage changes are computed from selectively chosen baseline years, no adjustment is made for several hundred tests, and bivariable results sit in an unread supplement.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Roughly half of sampled households yield a completed interview; handled only through standard weighting, which cannot correct for differential non-response among people using drugs heavily.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a prevalence study this is near the practical ceiling for national self-report data: a large probability sample, a consistent instrument, appropriate complex-survey analysis and explicit statements of the frame's exclusions. The constraints that matter are systematic undercount (the excluded populations and self-report) and the mortality comparison, which is drawn from a different, unlinked data source with its own coding undercount. The internal reporting choices (baseline years, period comparisons presented as single-year changes) affect the paper's headline numbers rather than the underlying estimates, which are printed with intervals in Table 1.

what_would_settle_it: Linkage of survey or treatment records to death certificates (or a cohort with repeated measurement of use patterns and mortality follow-up) would show whether the people whose use intensified are the people dying, and toxicological confirmation of the drugs involved in each death, together with sampling that includes unsheltered and incarcerated populations, would remove the main sources of undercount.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 195,711 NSDUH respondents aged 18 to 64 across 2015 to 2019 (weighted 50.9% women; 60.6% White, 18.0% Hispanic, 12.6% Black). Annual mean weighted response rates: screening 75.3%, interview 67.3%.

Overdose deaths involving psychostimulants other than cocaine among adults aged 18 to 64 rose from 5,526 in 2015 to 15,489 in 2019 (+180%, P for trend <0.001). Deaths also involving opioids rose from 2,306 to 8,438 (+266%); without opioids, from 3,220 to 7,051 (+119%); with cocaine, from 370 to 1,772 (+379%); without opioids or cocaine, from 3,102 to 6,698 (+116%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Trends in Psychostimulant-Involved Overdose Deaths; Table 1
key_findings.note: Coding is ICD-10 T43.6 with an overdose underlying cause; the authors note that 85% to 90% of such certificates mention methamphetamine and that about 6% of overdose certificates in 2019 named no drug.
The paper's 43% increase is 2016 to 2019; the 2015 to 2019 change is +22% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Past-year methamphetamine use disorder (thousands): 741 (578-905) in 2015, 672 (539-805) in 2016, 1,091 (816-1,365) in 2019 (P for trend 0.003). Use disorder without injection: 549 (417-682), 397 (299-496) and 815 (598-1,033) (P for trend 0.006).
key_findings.note: The paper's 62% and 105% increases are from 2016; from 2015 they are +47% and +48% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine injection did not change significantly: 321 (224-418) thousand in 2015, peaking at 472 (352-591) in 2017 and 365 (257-473) in 2019 (P=0.07, quadratic trend).

Frequent use (100 or more days in the past year) among adults who used methamphetamine: 649 (551-747) thousand in 2015, 615 (512-717) in 2016, 1,021 (860-1,183) in 2019 (P for trend 0.002), that is +57% from 2015 and the +66% quoted in the abstract from 2016 (editors' calculation).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Trends in Frequent Methamphetamine Use

key_findings.finding: Co-use: methamphetamine with cocaine rose from 402 (306-499) thousand in 2015 to 645 (477-813) in 2019 (+60%, P for trend 0.001). Methamphetamine with opioid misuse rose from 696 (556-836) to 865 (653-1,077) (P for trend 0.03), with the 2019 estimate similar to 2015 to 2018.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Trends in Methamphetamine Use, Co-Use, MUD, and Injection

key_findings.finding: Among adults reporting past-year methamphetamine use, the proportion with a use disorder or injection exceeded the proportion using without either in each year from 2017 to 2019 (60% to 67%, about 1,118,000 to 1,181,000 people, versus 37% to 40%, about 556,000 to 790,000; P for trend at most 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Trends in Methamphetamine Use, Co-Use, MUD, and Injection, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Adjusted prevalence of methamphetamine use disorder without injection, comparing the pooled 2015-2017 and 2018-2019 periods: 0.15% to 0.60% at ages 18 to 23 (+300%); 0.24% to 0.79% at 24 to 34; 0.39% to 0.85% at 35 to 49; 0.35% to 0.77% at 50 to 64; 0.29% to 0.80% in homosexual or bisexual men; 0.21% to 0.71% in lesbian or bisexual women; 0.29% to 0.79% in heterosexual men; 0.24% to 0.74% in heterosexual women; 0.06% to 0.64% in Black respondents (+967%); 0.28% to 0.78% in White respondents; 0.39% to 0.82% in Hispanic respondents; 0.36% to 0.80% in Asian or Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander respondents (all P<0.02).
key_findings.locator: Results › Increases in Adjusted Past-Year Prevalence of MUD Without Injection; Figure
key_findings.note: These are adjusted prevalences from pooled two- and three-year periods, not single-year estimates; the abstract presents them as changes 'from 2015 to 2019'. The underlying values are in the Figure, which is an image; the percentages above are those printed in the text.

key_findings.finding: Adjusted risk ratios for methamphetamine use disorder without injection (versus no methamphetamine use): past-year probation or parole 4.26 (3.25-5.58); HIV/AIDS 4.50 (2.60-7.80); American Indian or Alaska Native 9.98 (4.16-23.95), Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander 6.15 (2.10-17.95), Hispanic 5.13 (2.72-9.66) and White 3.98 (2.43-6.52) versus Black respondents; less than high school education 2.80 (1.48-5.32); Medicaid only 2.51 (1.76-3.58) and uninsured 1.93 (1.37-2.72) versus private insurance; household income under $20,000 1.77 (1.28-2.45); two or three moves in the past year 1.50 to 1.55; past-year major depressive episode 1.58 (1.19-2.12); suicidal ideation 1.62 (1.09-2.41); nicotine dependence 2.08 (1.56-2.78); cannabis 3.18 to 3.27; cocaine 2.37 (1.76-3.18); opioid misuse 2.31 (1.78-3.00).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, middle column; Table 2 for the corresponding adjusted prevalences

key_findings.finding: Adjusted risk ratios for methamphetamine injection (versus no methamphetamine use): past-year heroin injection 9.97 (6.43-15.47); homosexual men versus heterosexual women 3.66 (2.17-6.16); three moves in the past year 3.02 (2.25-4.05); probation or parole 2.74 (2.02-3.72); HIV/AIDS 3.36 (1.45-7.79); hepatitis B or C 2.46 (1.66-3.67); opioid misuse 3.40 (2.13-5.41); small metropolitan area 2.10 (1.61-2.76) versus large; ages 35 to 49 and 50 to 64 about 4.1 to 4.2 versus 18 to 23.

Among adults who used methamphetamine in the past year, adjusted prevalence of frequent use was 53.84% (47.82-59.76) with a use disorder without injection and 52.68% (45.50-59.75) with injection, versus 32.59% (28.12-37.41) with use alone (adjusted risk ratios 1.65, 1.42-1.92 and 1.62, 1.35-1.94). Frequent use was also more likely with hepatitis B or C (57.94%, ARR 1.33), a past-year sexually transmitted infection (56.76%, 1.29), hallucinogen use (54.65%, 1.28) and older age (55.74% at 50 to 64, 1.60), and less likely with past-year cocaine use (33.48%, 0.66), alcohol use disorder (34.96%, 0.74) and major depressive episode (40.04%, 0.84).
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Adjusted Prevalence and Correlates of Frequent Use

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine use disorder in this analysis is derived from DSM-IV criteria as implemented in NSDUH, not DSM-5, although the paper uses the DSM-5 term throughout and describes its symptoms in DSM-5 language.

Stated limitations: the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; the survey excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people and so probably underestimates use, use disorder, injection and frequency; self-report is subject to recall and social-desirability bias; and overdose deaths exclude deaths from methamphetamine-associated conditions such as stroke, myocardial infarction, pulmonary hypertension, HIV/AIDS and hepatitis, so methamphetamine-associated mortality is markedly underestimated.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline percentage increases are computed from the lowest year of the series rather than from 2015, while being described as changes from 2015 to 2019. From Table 1: any use 1,612 thousand in 2015 and 1,381 in 2016, so the stated 43% increase ('from 1.4 million') is 2016 to 2019, and the 2015 to 2019 change is +22%; use disorder without injection 549 in 2015 and 397 in 2016, so the stated 105% is +48% from 2015; methamphetamine use disorder overall, stated 62%, is +47% from 2015; frequent use, stated 66%, is +57% from 2015; methamphetamine use without opioid misuse, stated 61%, is +21%; without opioids or cocaine, stated 58%, is +9%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The most-quoted figures in the paper overstate growth from the first year of the series, in some cases by a factor of six. Claims in the encyclopedia should give both the year-specific estimates with their intervals and the baseline year actually used. The trend P values in Table 1 are based on the full five-year series and are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that methamphetamine use without a use disorder or injection 'increased 42% (from 556,000 to 790,000)' uses the 2017 value as the baseline; the 2015 value is 742,000, giving a 2015 to 2019 change of about +6%.
reporting_issues.consequence: This measure barely changed over the study period, which matters because the paper's argument is that use shifted towards riskier patterns; using 2017 as the baseline makes the non-disordered group appear to grow at a similar rate to the disordered group.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports subgroup changes in adjusted prevalence 'From 2015 to 2019', while the results section states these compare the pooled 2015-2017 period with the pooled 2018-2019 period.
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup increases (for example 0.06% to 0.64% among Black respondents) are period-to-period comparisons of adjusted estimates, not single-year values, and should be cited as such.

reporting_issues.issue: The exposure is called 'methamphetamine use disorder' and described with DSM-5 symptom language in the statistical-analysis section, while the measures section states the disorders were estimated with DSM-IV criteria.
reporting_issues.consequence: The construct is DSM-IV abuse or dependence as implemented in NSDUH; comparisons with DSM-5-based estimates from other sources are not like-for-like.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion reports that psychostimulant-involved overdose deaths more than doubled among adults aged 18 to 23 and roughly tripled in the older age groups 'from our additional analysis', but these numbers appear in no table or figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: An age-specific mortality analysis is used to support the paper's central argument but cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The key-points summary states that 'methamphetamine use disorder without injection doubled overall and increased 10-fold among Black individuals', mixing a national count change (computed from 2016) with an adjusted period-to-period prevalence ratio in a subgroup.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two different quantities are presented in one sentence; the 10-fold figure is an adjusted prevalence ratio between pooled periods with a baseline of 0.06%, which carries wide uncertainty (the Figure shows standard errors but no intervals in the text).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 marks several estimates as significantly different from the corresponding 2019 estimate, and these are exactly the years used as baselines for the percentage increases.
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentage changes appear to have been anchored to whichever year differed significantly from 2019, which is a form of selective baseline choice; the direction of the trends is nonetheless supported by the formal trend tests.

reporting_issues.issue: Numbers of overdose deaths and survey estimates are presented side by side in Table 1 with no common denominator, and the survey excludes institutionalized and unsheltered people while the death counts do not.
reporting_issues.consequence: Any ratio of deaths to people who use methamphetamine computed from this table would be biased upwards; the paper does not compute such a ratio but the juxtaposition invites it.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8459304 (all sections, Tables 1 to 4 with footnotes rendered as text, author contributions, conflict-of-interest, funding, role-of-funder and disclaimer statements read; the Figure is an image and its values were taken only from the text; the supplementary eTable of bivariable results was not read)
